Greenland
GREEN-land
n. (the Arctic island where the Norse church died out and Hans Egede began the Protestant mission to the Inuit in 1721)
Norse Grœnland, the green land, named by Erik the Red about 985 to attract settlers; Greenlandic Kalaallit Nunaat.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Greenland holds the one case in the north of a Christian church that simply disappeared, and the mission that went to look for it. Norse settlers had come about 985, built churches and a cathedral at Gardar, had a bishop, paid tithes to Rome, and then ceased: contact failed in the fifteenth century, the colonies died out, and when Europeans returned there were no Norsemen. Hans Egede, a Norwegian Lutheran pastor of Vagan, spent thirteen years petitioning Denmark to let him go and find them, sailed in 1721, found only Inuit, and turned to them instead. He stayed fifteen years, learned Kalaallisut, fought the whalers' brandy trade, buried his wife, and saw a smallpox epidemic in 1733 and 1734 kill a great part of the people he had come to; his son Paul Egede carried the work on and published the Greenlandic New Testament in 1766. The Moravians arrived in 1733 under Christian David and settled New Herrnhut beside him, and the two missions worked the same coast with some friction and much overlap. The dictionary enters Greenland because Egede went for one purpose, found it impossible, and did the harder thing he had not planned for, which is most of what missionary history actually consists of.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a mission as a sending with commission to preach; a colony as a body of people settled in a distant country; brandy as a spirit distilled from wine; and a pestilence as a contagious disease.

expand to see more

MISSION, n. A sending; persons sent with commission, as to preach the gospel in heathen lands.

COLONY, n. A company or body of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province.

BRANDY, n. A spirit distilled from wine; a strong spirituous liquor.

PESTILENCE, n. Plague; pest; any contagious or infectious disease that is epidemic and mortal.

CATECHUMEN, n. One who is receiving rudimentary instruction in the doctrines of Christianity.

Mar 16:15 — "And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature."

Act 16:7 — "After they were come to Mysia, they assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not."

Act 16:10 — "And after he had seen the vision, immediately we endeavoured to go into Macedonia, assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us for to preach the gospel unto them."

Modern Corruption

Arctic island where the Norse church died out, and where Hans Egede began the Protestant mission to the Inuit in 1721 and Paul Egede printed their New Testament in 1766.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the drink trade that followed every northern mission and undid much of it. Egede's letters complain constantly of the whalers and traders who sold brandy along the coast, and the dictionary names that commerce for what it was: men from Christian nations making money by ruining the people a Christian minister had come to teach. The brandy, and then the smallpox brought in on a ship, cost more Greenlandic lives than any doctrine saved in Egede's lifetime, and an honest mission history says so.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the redirection of a servant's plan by providence. Egede went to find lost Norsemen and was not permitted to; Paul and his company “assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not” (Act 16:7), and were sent to Macedonia instead, “assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us for to preach the gospel unto them” (Act 16:10). The commission is broad enough to cover the change, being to “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15), and the gospel is to be preached “to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people” (Rev 14:6), the Inuit as truly as the Norse.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek euangelion (G2098), the gospel; Greek sumbibazo (G4822), to conclude, to gather together; Greek ktisis (G2937), a creature.

expand to see more

Greek euangelion (G2098) — good news, the gospel; “preach the gospel to every creature”, Mark 16:15.

Greek ktisis (G2937) — a creature, a thing created; “to every creature”, Mark 16:15.

Greek peirazo (G3985) — to attempt, to try; “they assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not”, Acts 16:7.

Greek sumbibazo (G4822) — to conclude by putting together; “assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us”, Acts 16:10.

Greek phule (G5443) — a tribe, a kindred; “to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people”, Revelation 14:6.

Usage

"“they assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not” (Act 16:7) — Egede sailing in 1721 to find Norsemen and finding Inuit."

"“to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people” (Rev 14:6) — the Greenlandic New Testament of 1766."

"“preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15) — fifteen years on the coast, and a smallpox epidemic in 1733."
